trigger_or_context: You look back and see a pattern of bad matches.
review_reason: outcome-level; no discrete behavior to change

trigger_or_context: Early on, you notice something that worries you.
short_term_function: Ignoring the warning lets you keep dating the person instead of stopping.
developmental_cost: You end up choosing with less real proof.
adaptive_alternative_1: When something worries you, name what you saw. Then watch it or ask about it before you get more serious.
what_new_response_supports: You learn if the worry is a one-time thing or a real pattern.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You may sit with the chance a hopeful match won't work out.
context_conditions: If a warning is about your safety, get safe — don't test it.
review_reason: context (safety vs ordinary concern)

trigger_or_context: The relationship isn't working, and you keep staying.
short_term_function: Staying keeps the relationship going.
developmental_cost: You wait so long that your choice comes late.
adaptive_alternative_1: Pick ahead of time what you need to see, and by when. Then look at what really happened and act on it.
what_new_response_supports: You see if things are truly changing or just hoped for.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You may face a hard choice or a loss.
context_conditions: Staying is fine if real change is happening; not if it's only hope.
review_reason: context (repair vs hope)

trigger_or_context: You feel drawn to people who are hard to reach.
short_term_function: Function unclear from available evidence.
developmental_cost: You keep landing in the same spot, so you learn little about who fits you.
adaptive_alternative_1: Notice how much the other person shows up for you — texts back, keeps plans, treats you well. Give more only as they show more.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if they can really meet you back, or not.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Someone steady may feel less exciting at first.
context_conditions: You still get to feel drawn to someone; this is about pacing, not forcing.
review_reason: function unclear; near outcome-level

trigger_or_context: You look back and see the same relationship again and again.
review_reason: outcome-level; mechanism unspecified

trigger_or_context: Someone starts getting close to you.
short_term_function: Pushing people away keeps distance instead of letting closeness grow.
developmental_cost: You don't get to find out if this person is safe to be close to.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you feel the urge to push someone away, pause. Share one small, true thing and watch how they treat it before you pull back.
what_new_response_supports: You get to see, step by step, if this person is safe with the real you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Staying close feels risky, and you might get hurt.
context_conditions: If someone has shown they are not safe, keeping distance is wise. This is about pushing away safe people too.
review_reason: Safety context: distance is wise when someone is truly unsafe.

trigger_or_context: Someone tries to get close to you.
short_term_function: Blocking closeness keeps people from seeing the private parts of you.
developmental_cost: You never learn who could be trusted with the real you.
adaptive_alternative_1: Let one person in a little at a time. Share something real and small, then notice how they treat it.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if closeness is safe with this person, a little at a time.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Being seen feels scary.

trigger_or_context: A relationship starts to feel real, and you fear being left.
short_term_function: Leaving first means you end it instead of waiting to be left.
developmental_cost: You never find out if they would have stayed.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you want to leave first, name what is making you want to pull away, and whether any reason is a real dealbreaker or just a way to make distance. Then wait and watch how they show up before you decide.
what_new_response_supports: You get real proof of whether they stay or go, instead of guessing.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Waiting means sitting with the fear of being left.

trigger_or_context: You are getting to know someone new.
short_term_function: Keeping your guard up means you don't have to risk being open.
developmental_cost: People can't reach you, so you can't tell who is actually safe.
adaptive_alternative_1: If your guard is up with everyone by default, try lowering it in one small way with someone who has felt safe. Share a real thought and see how they respond.
what_new_response_supports: You start to learn who is safe to be open with.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Being open leaves you more exposed.
context_conditions: Guarding is wise if someone has shown they are not safe. This is about a guard that stays up with everyone, all the time.
review_reason: Context-dependent; guarding can be protective when danger is real.

trigger_or_context: Things are going well in a relationship.
short_term_function: Function unclear from available evidence
review_reason: Outcome-level label ('sabotage'); names no single behavior that can be changed.

trigger_or_context: Something bothers you or you two do not agree. A hard talk could happen.
short_term_function: Staying quiet keeps things calm right now and stops the hard talk from happening.
developmental_cost: The problem never gets worked out. The other person may not know something is wrong.
adaptive_alternative_1: When something bothers you, pick a calm moment. Name one thing you saw and one thing you need.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if the two of you can work through hard things together.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: The talk may feel uncomfortable. They may not take it well.
context_conditions: If speaking up is not safe, like if the other person gets mean or scary, your safety comes first.
review_reason: Safety context — avoiding conflict can be protective when the other person is unsafe.

trigger_or_context: A problem needs to be named. You notice you are the one who always brings it up.
short_term_function: Bringing things up gets the problem named instead of letting it sit.
developmental_cost: You carry all the work of raising hard things. You cannot tell if they would ever start one.
adaptive_alternative_1: If you keep being the only one who brings things up, say that out loud. Then leave room to see if they start too.
what_new_response_supports: You see if the work of raising hard things can be shared, or stays only on you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: They may not step up. You sit with not raising every little thing yourself.
context_conditions: Bringing things up is healthy. This is about the balance, not about going silent.
review_reason: Meaning depends on the balance of who raises issues; function is partly inferred.

trigger_or_context: After dating feels tiring or lets you down, you don't feel like getting the apps again.
short_term_function: Stepping back from the apps gives you a break from dating that feels hard right now.
developmental_cost: If the break is really you giving up, you stop meeting new people and stay stuck feeling low about dating.
adaptive_alternative_1: Notice if not getting the apps is a rest you chose, or a way to avoid dating because it feels hopeless. Pick how long you want to rest, then check in with yourself.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if you truly need a break or if you're just worn down, and you get to choose on purpose.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Sitting with the tired, let-down feeling instead of just avoiding it.
context_conditions: Resting on purpose is healthy. Pulling back because you feel it's hopeless can keep you stuck.
review_reason: Context-dependent and close to a feeling; meaning depends on whether the break is chosen rest or avoidance.

trigger_or_context: You want to connect or get things going. You notice you are always the one who starts it.
short_term_function: Starting things keeps you two connected instead of letting it go quiet.
developmental_cost: You carry all the work of reaching out. You cannot tell if they would ever start on their own.
adaptive_alternative_1: If you notice you always start things, pause sometimes. Say you would like them to reach out too, then leave room to see if they do.
what_new_response_supports: You see if starting things can be shared, or stays only on you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: They may not step up. You sit with the quiet while you wait.
context_conditions: Starting things is not bad. This is about balance, not about going cold.
review_reason: Meaning depends on the balance of who initiates; function is partly inferred.

trigger_or_context: After a breakup, you feel a strong pull to know what your ex is doing.
short_term_function: Checking their pages lets you keep an eye on their life, so it feels like you have not fully let go.
developmental_cost: You keep pulling them back into your day. The hurt stays fresh, and healing takes longer.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you feel the urge to check, name what you are feeling first. Then wait it out, or mute their page for a set time, and watch how each day goes.
what_new_response_supports: You give the hurt room to fade. That helps you heal and slowly move on.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: At first you may feel more anxious, like you are missing out on their life.
context_conditions: If you must stay in touch for real reasons, like shared kids or money, keep only what you truly need.
review_reason: Recovery phase has no competencies in the framework, so the alternative cannot map to an existing competency (source gap). The move is grounded only in the Healing task.

trigger_or_context: When you want someone to like you, you change who you are to match what they seem to want.
short_term_function: Changing yourself to fit them helps you fit in and keep them interested right now.
developmental_cost: They meet a made-up version of you. You can't tell if you two really fit, and you lose track of what you want.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you catch yourself about to change to fit them, show a small true part of you instead — a real opinion, like, or need. Then watch how they take it.
what_new_response_supports: You learn if someone likes the real you, and if you two actually fit.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Showing the real you feels risky, and some people may step back.

trigger_or_context: After you talk or text, you feel unsure what it really meant.
short_term_function: Reading it again is a way to look for an answer on your own instead of asking.
developmental_cost: You spend time going over old words instead of getting new, real answers. The worry keeps going.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you catch yourself rereading, name the one thing you want to know. Then ask it in plain words, or wait and watch what they do next.
what_new_response_supports: You get a real answer instead of guessing from old words.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You may have to sit with not knowing for a bit, or hear an answer you don't like.

trigger_or_context: You are on a dating app. You match with people, but a lot of them never write back or the chat dies fast.
short_term_function: Matching keeps you active in the dating pool and keeps you trying instead of stopping.
developmental_cost: When you keep putting effort into matches who do not write back, you learn almost nothing real about anyone. It also wears you down.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you match with someone, watch to see if they actually write back and keep the chat going. Put your time into the ones who do. If a match stays quiet, let that show you where not to spend more effort.
what_new_response_supports: You find out who really shows up in a conversation. You spend your energy where there is real back-and-forth.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You may let go of quiet matches you were hoping would come around. That can feel like a small loss each time.
context_conditions: Matching with a lot of people is normal on apps. This is not about matching less. It is about where you put your energy after you match.
review_reason: Meaning is context dependent, and the short-term function needs some inference; the phrase 'who never respond' is partly an outcome the person does not control.

trigger_or_context: A relationship starts to get closer.
short_term_function: Pulling away puts space between you and the other person.
developmental_cost: You keep ending closeness before you can see what it could be.
adaptive_alternative_1: Next time you feel yourself pulling away, pause and name what happened right before. Watch for the pattern instead of just acting on it.
what_new_response_supports: You start to see what sets off the urge, so you can choose your next move.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Slowing down means feeling the pull without giving in to it.

trigger_or_context: Things are going okay, but you feel the urge to end it.
short_term_function: Finding a reason to leave gives you a way out, so you end it instead of staying.
developmental_cost: You may leave good connections before you know what they really are.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you find a reason to leave, write it down. Ask if it is a real dealbreaker or a way to make distance. Then watch a little longer before you decide.
what_new_response_supports: You learn which reasons are real and which come from fear.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Staying longer means sitting with doubt.
context_conditions: Some reasons to leave are real. This is about telling real dealbreakers apart from fear.
review_reason: Context-dependent; some reasons to leave are real dealbreakers.

trigger_or_context: You're with someone and there's a need or a task. You jump in and give a lot.
short_term_function: Giving a lot keeps things running and keeps the peace for now.
developmental_cost: You can't see if the other person will carry their share.
adaptive_alternative_1: Give at a steady, fair level. Then leave room for the other person to do their part.
what_new_response_supports: You see if they step up and share, or leave it to you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Things may not get done your way, or as fast.
review_reason: Function partly inferred; "too much" is subjective.

trigger_or_context: You're in something that isn't really working, but leaving feels hard. You stay.
short_term_function: Staying keeps the relationship going for now.
developmental_cost: You keep giving time to something that may not change.
adaptive_alternative_1: Pick ahead of time what you need to see to keep staying, and by when. Then look at what really happened and decide.
what_new_response_supports: You see if things are truly changing or just hoped for.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You may face a hard choice or a loss.
context_conditions: Staying is fine if things are really getting better; not if it's only hope.
review_reason: Context-dependent; no clean Expansion competency for a self-boundary on staying.

trigger_or_context: You have a need, but speaking up feels like too much. You push it down.
short_term_function: Ignoring your needs keeps things smooth and skips asking for more.
developmental_cost: The other person never learns what you need, so it can't get met.
adaptive_alternative_1: Notice one thing you need. Then say it out loud in a calm, clear way.
what_new_response_supports: The other person gets a real chance to meet it — and you see if they do.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: It can feel risky to ask; they might say no.
review_reason: No clean Expansion competency for voicing personal needs.

trigger_or_context: There's a load of tasks to handle. You take it all on yourself.
short_term_function: Doing it all keeps things done and avoids a fight over who does what.
developmental_cost: You can't see if the other person will share the work.
adaptive_alternative_1: Do your part, then stop. Leave the rest for the other person to pick up.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if they share the load, or leave it to you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Some things may not get done, or not on time.

trigger_or_context: After being cheated on, you feel unsure and afraid it will happen again.
short_term_function: Searching keeps you doing something instead of waiting for their actions to show over time.
developmental_cost: Constant watching keeps you scanning for threat, so trust cannot settle and you stay stuck.
adaptive_alternative_1: Instead of scanning for every sign, name what you need to see to feel safe. Then watch, over time, whether their real actions match it, and let that guide you.
what_new_response_supports: You learn if they are truly steady and safe now, based on what they really do over time.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You have to sit with not knowing for a while.
context_conditions: Watching real, steady actions over time can be wise. Scanning for threat all the time keeps the pattern going.
review_reason: Context-dependent: watchful observation for Wise Trust vs. anxious scanning; short-term function partly inferred from phase architecture.

trigger_or_context: After a betrayal, you worry about what they might be hiding.
short_term_function: Checking their phone lets you look for proof instead of sitting with not knowing.
developmental_cost: Searching keeps you in a loop of looking for proof, so trust does not rebuild and you cannot move on.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you feel the urge to search their phone, pause. Name what you need to feel safe and say it out loud. Then let their real, day-to-day actions answer it over time.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if trust can rebuild from real behavior, not from searching.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Not checking can feel scary, and you have to sit with not knowing.

trigger_or_context: The betrayal is still on your mind and you want it to feel okay.
short_term_function: Asking more questions keeps you searching for an answer that will make the pain stop.
developmental_cost: The questions reopen the hurt each time and never bring the peace you want, so you stay stuck.
adaptive_alternative_1: Before you ask, pause and ask yourself: will this answer really change what I decide, or just reopen the hurt? If it will not help, let it rest this time.
what_new_response_supports: You start to see which questions truly help and which only keep the pain going.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You have to sit with some questions that may never be answered.

trigger_or_context: The other person isn't showing up, and you push harder.
short_term_function: Chasing keeps the connection going from your side even when they don't answer.
developmental_cost: You give a lot before you know they'll give back.
adaptive_alternative_1: Reach out when you want to. Then leave space to see if they reach back before you do more.
what_new_response_supports: You see if they show up too, or not.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: No answer can be an answer, and that's hard to sit with.

trigger_or_context: You meet someone kind, and you brush them off.
short_term_function: Function unclear from available evidence.
developmental_cost: You may pass on good matches before you really check them.
adaptive_alternative_1: If you notice you're brushing off someone kind, ask if it's 'no real spark' or just unfamiliar. Give it a little more time before you decide.
what_new_response_supports: You see if real interest can grow.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Less spark at the start, and some not-knowing.
context_conditions: Real attraction still matters — this isn't about dating people you don't like.
review_reason: context; function unclear

trigger_or_context: You are waiting to hear back, and you can see when they were last online.
short_term_function: Checking gives you a small piece of info when you don't have a real answer yet.
developmental_cost: You watch their moves instead of getting real answers. The uneasy feeling keeps coming back.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you want to check their online time, stop and notice something real instead: do they reach out to you and follow through? Let that be your answer.
what_new_response_supports: You see if they really show up for you, not just whether they are online.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You give up the small hit of info. You may have to wait to see what they do.

trigger_or_context: Someone asks you for something. You want to say no, but you say yes.
short_term_function: Saying yes keeps the other person happy and avoids a fight.
developmental_cost: You keep doing things you don't want to do, and they never know.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you want to say no, pause. Then give a simple, honest no to one small thing.
what_new_response_supports: You see how the other person handles your no.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: They may feel let down or upset.
review_reason: Cross-Phase: no framework competencies exist to anchor the alternative.

trigger_or_context: A hard topic comes up. You steer around it instead of talking.
short_term_function: Avoiding the talk keeps the peace now and skips the hard feelings.
developmental_cost: The problem stays unsolved and the other person never hears it.
adaptive_alternative_1: Pick one hard thing. Bring it up in a short, calm way at a good time.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if you two can work through a hard topic, or not.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: The talk may feel uncomfortable.
review_reason: Cross-Phase: no framework competencies exist to anchor the alternative.

trigger_or_context: Something feels tense. You say sorry fast, even when it's not your fault.
short_term_function: Saying sorry a lot smooths things over fast and lowers tension.
developmental_cost: You take blame that isn't yours, which hides what really happened.
adaptive_alternative_1: Save "sorry" for when you really did something wrong. Other times, say what you mean plainly.
what_new_response_supports: You see what is truly your part and what is not.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: It may feel odd not to soften things.
review_reason: Cross-Phase: no framework competencies exist to anchor the alternative.

trigger_or_context: You feel unhappy about something, but you stay quiet to keep things calm.
short_term_function: Keeping the peace avoids a fight and keeps things calm for now.
developmental_cost: Your unhappiness stays hidden, so nothing can change.
adaptive_alternative_1: Name one thing that bothers you, in a calm and kind way, instead of smoothing it over.
what_new_response_supports: You see if the other person will listen and work with you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: The calm may break; there may be some tension.
review_reason: Cross-Phase: no framework competencies exist to anchor the alternative.

trigger_or_context: Something is wrong, but you act like it's fine.
short_term_function: Acting okay avoids hard talks and keeps things smooth.
developmental_cost: The real problem stays hidden and can't get fixed.
adaptive_alternative_1: Pick one true thing and say it to a safe person. Watch how they take it.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if the other person can handle the real you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: It feels exposed to drop the act.
review_reason: Cross-Phase: no framework competencies exist to anchor the alternative.

trigger_or_context: You need something from the other person, but you don't bring it up.
short_term_function: Not asking keeps things easy and avoids a possible no.
developmental_cost: Your needs go unmet because the other person never hears them.
adaptive_alternative_1: Pick one need. Ask for it in a clear, calm way.
what_new_response_supports: The other person gets a real chance to meet it — and you see if they do.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Asking can feel risky; they might say no.
review_reason: Cross-Phase: no framework competencies exist to anchor the alternative.

trigger_or_context: A problem comes up. You notice you are always the one who steps in to fix it.
short_term_function: Fixing it keeps things running and stops the problem from just sitting there.
developmental_cost: You carry all the fixing. The other person never has to help, and you get worn out.
adaptive_alternative_1: When a problem comes up, pause before you jump in. Name it out loud and leave room for the other person to help fix it.
what_new_response_supports: You see if fixing problems can be shared, or stays only on you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Problems may sit longer. They may not step in.
context_conditions: Some things really do need you. This is about not carrying every single thing alone.
review_reason: Function partly inferred; over-functioning maintains the one-sided load.

trigger_or_context: You have tried for a while and feel worn out. Nothing changed, so you stop putting in effort.
short_term_function: Stopping saves your energy after trying has not led to any change.
developmental_cost: The other person stops seeing what is wrong. The distance between you grows because no one is working on it.
adaptive_alternative_1: Instead of quietly stopping, name it. Say you have pulled back and why, and ask what would need to change.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if real change is still possible here, or not.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Nothing may change. You may have to face what that means.
context_conditions: If you have truly tried many times and named it, stepping back may be part of deciding, not just giving up.
review_reason: Can shade toward discernment after real repeated effort; context-sensitive.

trigger_or_context: Something feels unfair or one-sided. Instead of saying it, you add it to a list in your head.
short_term_function: Keeping score keeps a record of what feels unfair so it is not forgotten.
developmental_cost: The focus stays on old wrongs. It gets harder to move forward or feel close, and resentment grows.
adaptive_alternative_1: When something feels unfair, name that one thing out loud soon after. Ask for what you need instead of storing it.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if the unfair things can be worked on, instead of piling up.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Speaking up feels risky. They may not respond the way you hope.
context_conditions: Noticing unfairness is okay. This is about voicing it early instead of storing it all up.
review_reason: Function inferred from the Resentment context; keeping score maintains resentment.

trigger_or_context: You felt strong love for someone. At the same time, you saw big differences between you, like your values, your faith, or the future you each wanted.
short_term_function: Ignoring the differences let you keep the relationship and the good feelings, instead of facing that you two might not fit.
developmental_cost: You made a big choice with real facts pushed aside. The differences did not go away. They came back later and hurt more.
adaptive_alternative_1: Let the differences be real, even when you care a lot. Name them plainly to yourself. Then look at whether you both can truly live with them.
what_new_response_supports: You get an honest picture of what is true. That helps you accept what happened and see a mismatch clearly instead of loving past it.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: It hurts to admit that love may not be enough. You have to feel that loss and maybe make a hard choice.
context_conditions: Having some differences is normal. This is about not pushing aside the big ones just because feelings are strong.
review_reason: Retrospective, past-tense wording; the alternative is a discernment-style derivation placed inside the Expiration/Acceptance task.

trigger_or_context: You want to talk or connect. You notice you are always the one who texts first.
short_term_function: Texting first keeps the contact going instead of waiting and wondering.
developmental_cost: You carry all the reaching out. You cannot tell if they would text you on their own.
adaptive_alternative_1: Notice if you are always first. Sometimes wait and leave room to see if they reach out to you too.
what_new_response_supports: You see if the effort goes both ways, or only from you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: They may not reach out. You sit with the quiet and the not-knowing.
context_conditions: Texting first is fine sometimes. This is about whether it is ever returned.
review_reason: Reciprocity function is partly inferred; meaning depends on the balance of effort.

trigger_or_context: You want to spend time together. You notice you are always the one making the plans.
short_term_function: Making the plans keeps you two seeing each other instead of nothing happening.
developmental_cost: You carry all the planning. You cannot tell if they would plan time with you.
adaptive_alternative_1: If you notice you plan everything, hold back sometimes. Leave room to see if they make a plan too.
what_new_response_supports: You see if making time together is shared, or only your job.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Plans may not happen. You sit with the not-knowing.
context_conditions: Making plans is fine. This is about whether it goes both ways.
review_reason: Reciprocity function is partly inferred; meaning depends on the balance of effort.

trigger_or_context: You put in a lot of effort with people and it feels one-sided, like you are chasing them.
short_term_function: Function unclear from available evidence
developmental_cost: This is a feeling about the effort, not one clear action. There is no single behavior here to change yet.
review_reason: Outcome/feeling-level statement ("I feel like I'm chasing"); does not name one discrete alterable behavior.

trigger_or_context: You care about someone. You notice you keep giving more than you get back.
short_term_function: Giving more keeps the relationship going and keeps them close, at least from your side.
developmental_cost: You pour in more than comes back. You cannot tell if they would give more on their own, and you get drained.
adaptive_alternative_1: Notice how much they give back. Match your giving to what returns, instead of always giving more.
what_new_response_supports: You see if the giving can go both ways, or stays one-sided.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Giving less may feel wrong at first. You may see they do not step up.
context_conditions: Giving is good. This is about balance — you still get to be generous when it is mutual.
review_reason: Reciprocity function is partly inferred; meaning depends on the balance of effort.

trigger_or_context: You get a gut feeling that something is off.
short_term_function: Ignoring the feeling means you don't have to act on it or bring it up.
developmental_cost: You stop trusting your own read, which is the heart of this pattern.
adaptive_alternative_1: Treat the feeling as a clue. Name what set it off, sort facts from your story, then watch or ask.
what_new_response_supports: You start trusting your read again, based on facts.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You might be wrong, and you have to sit with the feeling.
context_conditions: A gut feeling is a clue to check, not a rule to obey.
review_reason: context (intuition is data, not proof)

trigger_or_context: You already saw clear warning signs.
short_term_function: Staying let you keep the relationship instead of ending it over the worry.
developmental_cost: You act against what you already knew, so your judgment counts for less.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you notice a real worry, use it to check and decide — not to push past it.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if the worry is a dealbreaker or not.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You may have to make a hard choice.
review_reason: retrospective wording (borders belief)

trigger_or_context: Someone lets you down, and you give another chance.
short_term_function: Another chance keeps the relationship going for now.
developmental_cost: Open-ended chances put off your choice.
adaptive_alternative_1: If you give another chance, name one real change you need to see, and by when. Then look at what happened.
what_new_response_supports: You see if the change is real or just hoped for.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Holding a limit is hard, and it might end.
context_conditions: Fixing things and just waiting are not the same — this depends on whether they own their part.
review_reason: context (repair vs enabling)

trigger_or_context: A hard or touchy thing comes up in the relationship that needs to be talked about.
short_term_function: Bringing it up means the hard stuff gets talked about instead of being ignored.
developmental_cost: You carry the whole job of starting hard talks. Your partner never has to, so you can't see if they would step up too. Doing it alone can wear you down.
adaptive_alternative_1: Keep bringing up things that matter. But once, name the pattern out loud. Tell your partner you'd like the job of starting hard talks to be shared. Then leave a little room and watch if they ever start one too.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if your partner can carry some of this too, or if it always falls on you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Some hard things may sit a bit longer while you wait to see if they speak up. Holding back can feel uncomfortable.
context_conditions: Bringing up hard things is healthy — this is not about going quiet. It is about whether you are always the only one. If a real problem needs to be raised now, raise it.
review_reason: Context-dependent behavior; the short-term function and the competency mapping both needed judgment.

trigger_or_context: You still feel hurt by something that happened before.
short_term_function: Bringing up the past keeps the hurt out in the open instead of letting it rest.
developmental_cost: Going back to the past again and again keeps you re-living the hurt, so it is hard to accept it and move forward.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you feel pulled to bring up the past, notice it. Ask if there is one real thing that still needs to be worked out. If not, let it rest and speak to what is happening now.
what_new_response_supports: You see whether something real still needs repair, or whether you are re-living an old hurt.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Letting the past rest can feel like you are letting them off the hook.

trigger_or_context: A relationship isn't right, but ending it means being alone.
short_term_function: Staying meant you didn't have to be alone.
developmental_cost: You spend time in something that isn't right for you.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you notice you're staying just to not be alone, name that. Then look at whether the relationship is good for you apart from not wanting to be alone.
what_new_response_supports: You choose to stay or go based on fit, not just to avoid being alone.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You may have to face being alone for a while.
review_reason: Retrospective statement; function is stated by the person.

trigger_or_context: You aren't sure how much the other person cares.
short_term_function: Testing them gave you proof of their feelings without having to ask.
developmental_cost: Tests can push people away and still don't give a clear answer.
adaptive_alternative_1: Instead of testing, say what you need out loud. Then watch how they respond to a real request.
what_new_response_supports: You get a real answer to a real ask, instead of a guess from a test.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Asking straight out risks a clear no.
review_reason: Retrospective (past tense) statement.

trigger_or_context: You can tell the relationship isn't healthy.
short_term_function: Staying let you keep the relationship instead of ending it over what you already knew.
developmental_cost: You spend time in something you already know isn't good for you.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you notice you already know something isn't healthy, say it plainly to yourself. Use what you see to decide, instead of pushing past it.
what_new_response_supports: You act on what you already see instead of ignoring it.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Acting on what you know may mean a hard ending.
context_conditions: Some things really are unhealthy. This is about acting on what you see, not ignoring real problems.
review_reason: Retrospective; borders on outcome-level ('wasn't healthy').

trigger_or_context: Something in the relationship is wrong or letting you down.
short_term_function: Waiting keeps the relationship going for now and lets you put off a hard choice.
developmental_cost: You make choices based on what you hope for, not on what is really happening.
adaptive_alternative_1: Look at what has really changed, not what you hope will change. Pick what you need to see, and by when. Then decide based on what really happened.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if things are really getting better or if you are only hoping.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You may face a hard choice or a loss.
context_conditions: Waiting is fine if you can see real, steady change. It keeps the pattern going if it is only hope.
review_reason: Context-dependent: meaning turns on whether real change is visible; short-term function partly inferred from phase architecture.

trigger_or_context: The other person does something that lets you down or worries you.
short_term_function: Making excuses lets you keep seeing them in a good light instead of facing what they did.
developmental_cost: You judge them by the story you tell, not by what they really do.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you catch yourself explaining away what they did, name what actually happened first. Then decide what it means to you.
what_new_response_supports: You see their actions clearly, based on what really happened.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Facing it plainly can hurt.

trigger_or_context: You have raised something before. Nothing shifted, so you go quiet.
short_term_function: Going quiet saves your effort when talking has not led to any change.
developmental_cost: The other person stops hearing what is wrong. Nothing can shift because it is no longer named.
adaptive_alternative_1: Instead of going quiet, name the pattern. Say you have raised this before and nothing changed, and ask what would need to shift.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if real change is possible here, or not.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: They may still not change. You may have to face what that means.
context_conditions: If you have truly named it many times and nothing changes, going quiet may be part of deciding, not just giving up.
review_reason: Can shade toward discernment after repeated genuine attempts; context-sensitive.

trigger_or_context: A hard conversation is needed. It feels tiring, so you skip it.
short_term_function: Skipping the talk saves your energy and spares you the tiring conversation right now.
developmental_cost: Hard things stay unsolved. The other person may not know it matters to you.
adaptive_alternative_1: Pick one hard thing and a calm time. Keep it short: say what is wrong and one thing you need.
what_new_response_supports: You learn if hard talks can be shorter and go somewhere, instead of always draining you.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Starting the talk takes energy. It may still feel hard.
context_conditions: If the talk is tiring because the other person is mean or scary, your safety comes first.
review_reason: Safety context — avoidance can be protective when the other person is unsafe.

trigger_or_context: The relationship has ended, but you still put your ring on.
short_term_function: Keeping the ring on keeps part of the bond close, so it feels like you have not fully let go.
developmental_cost: A daily reminder can keep the loss feeling fresh, so letting go and healing may take longer.
adaptive_alternative_1: Notice why the ring stays on right now. If it brings you comfort while you grieve, that is okay. If it keeps you from facing the loss, try setting it aside for a set time and watch how each day feels.
what_new_response_supports: You learn if the ring is helping you grieve or holding you back from healing.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Taking it off, even for a little while, can bring up sad or lonely feelings.
context_conditions: There is no set clock for grief. Wearing a ring to honor someone you loved or lost can be healthy. This is about your own healing, not a rule.
review_reason: Recovery phase has no competencies in the framework, so the alternative cannot map to an existing competency (source gap). Meaning is context dependent; the ring may comfort grief or delay letting go, and the move is grounded only in the Healing task.

trigger_or_context: A new relationship starts to go well.
short_term_function: Function unclear from available evidence
review_reason: Outcome-level label ('ruin'); names no single behavior that can be changed.

trigger_or_context: Someone gets close to you.
short_term_function: Pushing them away when they get close puts space back between you.
developmental_cost: You stop closeness right when it could grow.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you feel the push-away urge as someone gets close, pause. Stay with one small moment of closeness and notice how it feels.
what_new_response_supports: You learn whether closeness with this person is safe.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Closeness feels scary and exposing.

trigger_or_context: You aren't sure the other person will stay.
short_term_function: Testing gives you proof they'll stay without asking for what you need.
developmental_cost: Tests can wear people down and still don't give a clear answer.
adaptive_alternative_1: Instead of testing, name what you're afraid of and ask for what you need directly. Watch how they respond.
what_new_response_supports: You get a real answer instead of a guess from a test.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Asking straight out risks a clear no.

trigger_or_context: A relationship gets serious and you fear being left.
short_term_function: Leaving first means you end it instead of waiting to be left.
developmental_cost: You never find out if they would have stayed.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you want to leave first, name what is making you want to pull away, and whether any reason is a real dealbreaker or just a way to make distance. Then wait and watch how they show up before you decide.
what_new_response_supports: You get real proof of whether they stay, instead of guessing.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Waiting means sitting with the fear of being left.

trigger_or_context: You notice you keep blocking your own relationships.
short_term_function: Function unclear from available evidence
review_reason: Outcome-level; 'don't know how to stop' names no discrete behavior.

trigger_or_context: Something bothers you in a family relationship, and speaking up could cause tension.
short_term_function: Keeping the peace helps you avoid conflict and tension in the moment.
developmental_cost: Your own feelings and needs stay hidden, so others never learn what really bothers you.
adaptive_alternative_1: When something bothers you, say one true thing about how you feel. You do not have to fix it or fight. Just let your view be known.
what_new_response_supports: People get to know what you really think. You find out if the calm was real or just quiet.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Things may feel tense for a bit. Someone may not like hearing it.
context_conditions: Keeping the peace is fine at times. This is about when you always do it and hide how you feel. If a home is not safe, staying quiet can be a way to stay safe.
review_reason: Cross-Phase source gap: no competency cleanly maps and there is no single developmental task. This is a family context (Adult Children & Parents), so a safety condition is named.

trigger_or_context: You want to talk to a friend or make plans with them.
short_term_function: Reaching out first keeps the friendship going from your side.
developmental_cost: You never get to see if the friend would reach out too.
adaptive_alternative_1: Reach out when you want to. Then leave some space and see if they reach back before you reach again.
what_new_response_supports: You get to see if the friendship goes both ways, or only one way.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: It might feel quiet for a while. You may learn a friend will not reach back.
context_conditions: Reaching out first is fine sometimes. This is about when it is always you. A friend may also be going through a hard time.
review_reason: Cross-Phase source gap: no competency cleanly maps. Maintaining role is inferred from the one-sided-friendship context, so function is stated only in its narrow, supported form.

trigger_or_context: Something about the relationship feels open or unknown.
short_term_function: Having a plan helps you feel in control and eases the not-knowing right now.
developmental_cost: You push for certainty faster than the relationship can give it, so you don't get to see how it goes on its own.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you feel the pull to plan it all, name what feels unknown. Then let one small thing stay open and watch what happens.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if you can sit with some not-knowing. You get to see how the other person acts on their own.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: The open feeling is uncomfortable. You may not like not having an answer yet.
context_conditions: Plans are useful at times. This is about when you need one for everything and can't leave room to see how things unfold.
review_reason: Cross-Phase source gap: no competency cleanly maps and there is no single developmental task. The maintaining role fits the control pattern; alternative is observation/discernment-style.

trigger_or_context: A relationship is moving along at its own pace.
review_reason: Names a difficulty, not a discrete alterable behavior. It describes the trouble letting things unfold but not what you actually do, so it is outcome-level.

trigger_or_context: Things are going okay, but you expect they could go wrong.
short_term_function: Bracing ahead of time softens the blow if things do go wrong, so it feels safer right now.
developmental_cost: You stay guarded and hold back, so you don't let the relationship be what it really is.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you catch yourself bracing, name what you are afraid will happen. Then watch what really happens instead of acting on the fear.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if the worry is real or just a habit of guarding. You get to see how things actually go.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Staying open means you could be let down for real. That is a hard feeling to sit with.
context_conditions: Some caution is wise. This is about when you brace before there is any real sign of trouble.
review_reason: Cross-Phase source gap: no competency cleanly maps and there is no single developmental task. The maintaining role fits the control/self-protection pattern; alternative is observation-style.

trigger_or_context: A step forward comes up, like dating again or getting closer to someone. You do not feel ready yet.
short_term_function: Waiting until you feel ready lets you put off a step that feels scary.
developmental_cost: You stay in one place. You never find out how the step would really go.
adaptive_alternative_1: Pick one small step you can take now, even if you do not feel all the way ready. Take it and watch what you learn.
what_new_response_supports: You find out you can move before you feel fully ready. You learn from real steps, not just from waiting.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Acting before you feel ready feels uncomfortable.
review_reason: Cross-Phase behavior: no phase competency exists to ground the alternative (framework gap).

trigger_or_context: You have a choice about moving forward. You are not sure how it will turn out.
short_term_function: Trying to be sure first lets you put off a choice that could go wrong.
developmental_cost: You wait for a sure thing that may never come. So you do not move at all.
adaptive_alternative_1: Notice that some things cannot be known ahead of time. Check what you can now, choose with what you have, and let the rest show itself over time.
what_new_response_supports: You learn to move with 'enough' proof instead of waiting for perfect proof.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You have to move while some things are still unknown.
review_reason: Cross-Phase behavior: no phase competency exists to ground the alternative (framework gap).

trigger_or_context: Things are not okay inside. Someone asks how you are, or you feel you should look fine.
short_term_function: Acting okay lets you avoid showing the truth and having a hard talk about it.
developmental_cost: Nothing gets worked on. No one can see the real you or help.
adaptive_alternative_1: Try naming one true thing to one safe person, even if it is small. Watch how it feels and how they answer.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if it is safe to be honest. You stop carrying it all by yourself.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Being honest can feel exposing at first.
context_conditions: This is about being honest with a safe person, not telling everyone everything.
review_reason: Cross-Phase behavior: no phase competency exists to ground the alternative (framework gap).

trigger_or_context: You have a thought that might cause conflict.
short_term_function: Editing yourself keeps the peace and avoids conflict for now.
developmental_cost: The other person never meets the real you, so you can't tell if they'd accept you.
adaptive_alternative_1: Try sharing one honest thought you would usually hold back. Watch how they handle it.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if you can be real with this person.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Being honest may lead to conflict.

trigger_or_context: You feel something but aren't sure it's safe to say.
short_term_function: Keeping feelings in lets you avoid the risk of sharing them.
developmental_cost: The other person can't respond to what you never say.
adaptive_alternative_1: Say one real feeling out loud, even a small one. Notice how the other person responds.
what_new_response_supports: You learn whether it is safe to share with this person.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Sharing feelings feels exposing.

trigger_or_context: You are around someone you could be close to.
short_term_function: Function unclear from available evidence
review_reason: Metaphor/outcome-level ('wearing a mask'); names no discrete behavior.

trigger_or_context: You are with your partner, but you feel checked out, so you just do the usual day-to-day things.
short_term_function: Doing the motions keeps the relationship running as usual, so you don't have to stop and deal with what feels off.
developmental_cost: You stay side by side but not really together, so real closeness can't grow.
adaptive_alternative_1: When you notice you're on autopilot, pick one small moment to really show up. Name to yourself what you feel, then share one honest thing with your partner.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if real closeness can come back when you show up — or if the gap is bigger than a rough patch.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Showing up for real can feel scary after being checked out, and what you learn may be hard.
context_conditions: A short tired stretch where you still show up is different from being checked out for a long time. This is about the long, settled kind.
review_reason: No Expansion competency cleanly maps to bringing authentic emotional presence; behavior is also borderline between Likely Maintains and Context Dependent.

trigger_or_context: You grew up seeing certain ways of doing relationships. Now you want to do them in a new, healthier way.
short_term_function: Function unclear from available evidence
developmental_cost: This names a goal, not one clear action. There is no single behavior to look at, so there is no clear cost to point to.
review_reason: Insufficient evidence: the statement names a broad goal or effort ("trying to unlearn"), not one discrete, alterable behavior, so no behavioral chain can be built. It points toward change rather than maintaining a pattern. Also Cross-Phase/Renewal has no competencies in the framework (source gap).

trigger_or_context: You are getting more serious with someone. You are not sure yet if it will last.
short_term_function: Waiting to see gives you more time before you have to fully invest or decide.
developmental_cost: If you wait and never decide, you can stay stuck and never really commit.
adaptive_alternative_1: If you notice you are just waiting, name what you need to see and by when. Keep showing up while you watch. Then decide.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if the relationship is steady enough to invest in — or not.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You have to sit with not knowing, then make a real choice.
context_conditions: Watching over time is healthy. It only becomes a problem if you wait so long that you never decide or invest.
review_reason: Context-dependent: meaning depends on whether watching is active evaluation or an indefinite stall.

trigger_or_context: You are opening up to someone new and watching to see if it's safe.
short_term_function: Sharing a little at a time while watching for safety lets you test if it's safe to open up.
review_reason: Already serves Discernment; reinforcement candidate, no replacement needed.

trigger_or_context: The other person made promises, and you watch what they do.
short_term_function: Watching lets you see if their actions match their words.
context_conditions: This helps unless it turns into constant checking.

trigger_or_context: You are not sure you can count on this person, so you set up small tests.
short_term_function: Testing is a way to check if you can count on them without asking straight out.
developmental_cost: Secret tests can give mixed results. The other person doesn't know what you need, so you may not learn the truth.
adaptive_alternative_1: Instead of setting up a test, name one real thing you need. Ask for it in plain words. Then watch, over time, if they come through.
what_new_response_supports: You find out if they can really be counted on, based on real tries, not secret tests.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: You have to say what you need out loud. They might not come through, and that tells you something too.
review_reason: Maintaining call rests on reading 'testing' as hidden tests, not plain observing; candidate-section item with a second cluster, so the framing could shift.

trigger_or_context: You are coming out of a hard time. You have some energy back, and you are choosing to put it into your work.
short_term_function: Putting your energy into work helps you build your life back up instead of just getting by.
developmental_cost: No clear cost. This already helps you move forward after a hard time.
review_reason: Renewal phase has no competencies in the framework (source gap). This is a reinforcement candidate that already serves Reengagement, not a behavior to change.

trigger_or_context: You are getting to know someone new. You feel a pull to stay closed off so you don't get used again.
short_term_function: Staying guarded keeps you feeling safe. You don't have to risk getting used or hurt again.
developmental_cost: When your guard is always up, people never get a chance to show you who they really are. So you can't tell safe people from unsafe ones.
adaptive_alternative_1: Notice when your guard is up. Let it down a little in small, safe ways. Then watch how the person treats you before you open more.
what_new_response_supports: You get to see if this person is really safe, instead of guessing. You learn who has earned more of your trust.
expected_discomfort_or_cost: Letting your guard down even a little can feel scary. You may feel unsure for a while.
context_conditions: If someone has shown they hurt you, or your safety is at risk, keeping your guard up is smart. This is only about people who have not shown they are unsafe.
review_reason: Context-dependent: guardedness can be healthy pacing or a wall that blocks real information. The meaning depends on whether it is calibrated to what the person actually shows, so the alternative stays conditional.
